1. Hypertensive Heart Disease

Pathology of the Heart I · SDL + ELS

1.1 Diagnostic criteria

Hypertensive heart disease (HHD) requires both of the following:

#Criterion
1Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (without any other identifiable cause, e.g. aortic stenosis)
2History of systemic hypertension

1.2 Left-sided HHD: from pressure-overload to LA enlargement

Chronic hypertension raises resistance the LV must pump against (↑ afterload, pressure-overload). The heart compensates by cardiomyocyte hypertrophy — cells enlarge and add contractile proteins — producing concentric LVH (new sarcomeres added in parallel, thickening the wall without dilating the chamber).

This same hypertrophy stiffens the LV as interstitial connective tissue thickens alongside the myocytes. A stiff, non-compliant LV can't fill properly in diastole, so blood backs up into the left atrium → LA pressure-overload → LA hypertrophy/dilation by the same compensatory logic.

Why no ventricular dilation (early)? Left-sided HHD is a pressure-overload disease, not a volume-overload disease. Pressure-overload → concentric hypertrophy (parallel sarcomere addition, walls thicken, chamber size preserved). Volume-overload → eccentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in series, chamber dilates). Ventricular dilation can appear in late-stage HHD once the compensated heart begins to fail, but it is not a feature of early disease.

1.3 Right-sided HHD (cor pulmonale)

Acute or chronic lung disease (pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis) increases resistance in the pulmonary vasculature → pulmonary hypertension. This produces the same pressure-overload physiology on the right side that systemic hypertension produces on the left: RV pressure-overload → RV hypertrophy → can progress to right-sided heart failure, i.e. cor pulmonale.

Practice Questions — Section 1

1. A 61-year-old woman with a 15-year history of poorly controlled hypertension is found on echocardiogram to have a thickened, non-dilated left ventricular wall with preserved chamber diameter. Which best describes the mechanism producing this finding?

Explanation: Chronic hypertension is a pressure-overload state. Myocytes respond by adding sarcomeres in parallel, producing concentric hypertrophy (thick wall, normal-to-small chamber) rather than the chamber dilation seen with volume-overload (eccentric hypertrophy, sarcomeres added in series).

2. A patient with longstanding hypertensive heart disease develops left atrial enlargement. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

Explanation: Concentric LVH increases interstitial connective tissue alongside myocyte hypertrophy, stiffening the ventricle. The stiff LV cannot fill normally in diastole, so pressure backs up into the LA, which then hypertrophies/dilates in response to its own pressure-overload.

3. A patient with severe COPD and long-standing pulmonary hypertension develops right ventricular hypertrophy and eventually right heart failure. What is this clinical entity called?

Explanation: Cor pulmonale is right-sided heart disease (RVH progressing to RV failure) resulting from pulmonary hypertension driven by intrinsic lung disease — the same pressure-overload logic as left HHD, applied to the right side.

2. Pericardial Disease

Pathology of the Heart I · SDL + ELS

2.1 Types of acute pericarditis

TypeExudateCause(s)
SerousThin, clear, protein-richSLE, rheumatic fever, scleroderma, tumors, uremia
Fibrinous / serofibrinousStraw-colored, fibrinous (“bread and butter” pericardium)Acute MI, uremia, rheumatic fever, SLE, trauma, thoracic radiation
Suppurative / purulentPus-like, extensive neutrophilsBacterial or fungal infection
CaseousGranulomatous, caseousTuberculosis
HemorrhagicBlood in the exudate (malignant cells may be seen)Cancer (most often); can also be trauma or infection

2.2 Acute → chronic pericarditis

Unresolved acute inflammation stimulates a healing response → fibrosis and stiffening of the pericardium → chronic pericarditis. Chronic pericarditis can also arise directly from thoracic irradiation or cardiac surgery, both of which stimulate fibrosis independent of a prior acute episode.

2.3 Constrictive pericarditis vs. restrictive cardiomyopathy

Both present with impaired ventricular filling and similar clinical pictures, but they differ in tissue, cause, and treatment:

FeatureConstrictive PericarditisRestrictive Cardiomyopathy
Tissue affectedPericardiumMyocardium
CausesTuberculosis, prior acute pericarditis, cardiac surgery, thoracic radiationAmyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or idiopathic
TreatmentCan be treated surgically (pericardiectomy)Cannot be corrected surgically

2.4 Cardiac tamponade

Rapidly accumulating pericardial fluid compresses the heart, impairing ventricular filling, stroke volume, and cardiac output. Inadequate blood flow can progress quickly to hypotension, shock, and death — making tamponade a medical emergency. Speed of accumulation matters more than volume: a slow, chronic effusion can stretch the pericardium to accommodate a large volume, while a fast effusion of a much smaller volume can tamponade.

Practice Questions — Section 2

1. A patient with metastatic breast cancer develops a large pericardial effusion. Pericardiocentesis fluid is grossly bloody, and cytology shows clusters of atypical cells. Which type of pericarditis does this represent?

Explanation: Hemorrhagic pericarditis (blood within the exudate) is most often due to malignancy; malignant cells are frequently identifiable in the fluid, as in this case. Trauma and infection are less common causes.

2. A patient recovering from an acute MI three days ago develops new-onset chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. If a pericardial biopsy were obtained, which exudate pattern would be classically described?

Explanation: Post-MI (and post-cardiac injury) pericarditis is classically fibrinous/serofibrinous, producing the "bread and butter" shaggy appearance of the visceral and parietal pericardial surfaces.

3. Which feature best distinguishes constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy?

Explanation: Constrictive pericarditis is a pericardial (not myocardial) disease and is potentially surgically correctable via pericardiectomy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy affects the myocardium itself (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, idiopathic) and has no surgical fix.

3. Valvular Heart Disease: Stenosis & Insufficiency

Pathology of the Heart II · SDL + ELS

3.1 Stenosis vs. insufficiency: two different overload patterns

Stenosis = valve thickening/hardening that narrows the orifice → reduced forward flow → pressure-overload proximal to the valve → concentric hypertrophy.

Insufficiency (regurgitation) = a valve that cannot close completely → backward flow → volume-overload → eccentric hypertrophy & dilation.

LesionCause(s)Flow AbnormalityOverload / ChamberRemodeling
Aortic stenosisAge-related calcification, congenital bicuspid valve, rheumatic heart disease↓ LV→Ao flow in systolePressure-overload, LVConcentric LVH
Aortic insufficiencyAortic root dilation, connective tissue disorders, infective endocarditis, rheumatic heart diseaseBackward flow Ao→LV in diastoleVolume-overload, LVEccentric LVH + dilation
Mitral stenosisRheumatic heart disease (classic cause)↓ LA→LV flow in diastolePressure-overload, LALA dilation
Mitral insufficiencyMitral valve prolapse, infective endocarditis, “fen-phen,” rheumatic heart diseaseBackward flow LV→LA (+ forward LV→Ao) in systoleVolume-overload, LV (some LA too)Eccentric LVH + dilation

3.2 Mitral valve prolapse & myxomatous degeneration

The mitral valve has three connective-tissue layers: fibrosa (collagen), spongiosa (proteoglycans), and atrialis (elastin). In a connective tissue disorder, defective connective tissue synthesis leads to myxomatous degeneration — excess gel-like proteoglycan deposition expands the spongiosa layer and disorganizes the fibrosa/atrialis. The result is a redundant, floppy valve whose leaflets prolapse into the LA during systole.

3.3 Bicuspid aortic valve → aortic stenosis

A congenitally bicuspid aortic valve arises when two of the three cusps fail to separate, leaving one smaller and one larger cusp joined by a midline raphe. The raphe is a nucleation point for calcification, and increased mechanical stress across the abnormal valve accelerates fibrosis — both features that markedly accelerate the calcific aortic stenosis that would otherwise occur much later from age-related "wear and tear" alone.

Practice Questions — Section 3

1. A 58-year-old man has a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve found incidentally in his 30s. He now presents in his 50s with an early-peaking systolic ejection murmur and echocardiographic evidence of a heavily calcified, stenotic aortic valve. Why does a bicuspid valve accelerate this process?

Explanation: The raphe formed by the fused cusps serves as a nidus for calcium deposition, and the abnormal valve geometry increases mechanical stress across the leaflets, accelerating fibrosis and calcification well before the age typically seen with a normal trileaflet valve.

2. A patient with Marfan syndrome develops a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur. Echocardiogram shows a redundant, billowing mitral valve leaflet. Which histologic change underlies this finding?

Explanation: Myxomatous degeneration — proteoglycan-rich expansion of the spongiosa layer with disorganization of the fibrosa/atrialis — produces the classic redundant, floppy leaflet of mitral valve prolapse, common in connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome.

3. A patient in acute pulmonary edema is found to have severe mitral stenosis. Which chamber bears the primary pressure-overload from this lesion?

Explanation: Mitral stenosis restricts LA→LV flow during diastole, so the pressure-overload falls on the chamber upstream of the obstruction — the left atrium, which dilates in response (rather than hypertrophying, since atrial walls are thin).

4. Rheumatic Fever & Rheumatic Heart Disease

Pathology of the Heart II · SDL + ELS

4.1 Rheumatic fever vs. rheumatic heart disease

Rheumatic fever (RF) is an acute autoimmune disease that follows a group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngeal infection. Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is the chronic disease that develops from repeated bouts of RF: repeated inflammation/healing cycles scar and fibrose cardiac structures, especially the mitral valve.

4.2 Why GAS specifically?

The mechanism is molecular mimicry: antibodies and CD4+ T cells generated against streptococcal M protein cross-react with structurally similar human antigens (including cardiac antigens), triggering an autoimmune response. Other infections generate antibodies that typically do not cross-react with human tissue this way.

4.3 RF → RHD → mitral stenosis, step by step

Repeated inflammatory episodes damage the mitral valve; each round of healing lays down more fibrosis and calcification. Over years, this cycle produces extensive scarring and commissural fusion, narrowing the orifice into the classic “fish-mouth” stenotic mitral valve.

4.4 From rheumatic fever to stroke: the full pathophysiologic sequence

Mechanistic thread Mitral stenosis → ↑ LA pressure → LA dilation (compensation) → atrial fibrillation → blood stasis in the LA → thrombus formation → embolization → stroke. This single chain links a valve lesion all the way to a neurologic emergency, and is a favorite integrative board pattern.

4.5 Rheumatic fever is multisystem (Jones Criteria organ systems)

SystemManifestation
MusculoskeletalMigratory polyarthritis
IntegumentarySubcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum
NervousSydenham chorea
CardiovascularPancarditis (endocardium, myocardium, pericardium all involved)

Diagnosis (Modified Jones Criteria) requires evidence of a prior GAS infection AND either 2 major criteria, or 1 major + 2 minor criteria.

Practice Questions — Section 4

1. A 34-year-old woman develops migratory joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, and fever several weeks after an untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. A myocardial biopsy at this stage would most likely show which finding?

Explanation: This is acute rheumatic fever (migratory polyarthritis, subcutaneous nodules, fever, post-strep). The pathognomonic cardiac lesion at this stage is the Aschoff body, containing activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells).

2. Ten years after an episode of acute rheumatic fever, a patient develops atrial fibrillation and then a cardioembolic stroke. Which sequence best explains the link between her valve disease and the stroke?

Explanation: Rheumatic mitral stenosis raises LA pressure, causing LA dilation; the dilated, fibrotic atrium is prone to atrial fibrillation, which causes blood stasis (especially in the LA appendage) and thrombus formation that can embolize to the brain.

3. Why does infection with group A Streptococcus specifically predispose to rheumatic fever, while most other bacterial infections do not?

Explanation: The antibodies and CD4+ T cells raised against GAS M protein cross-react with structurally similar self-antigens, including those in cardiac tissue — molecular mimicry — producing an autoimmune carditis that most other infections do not trigger.

5. Infective & Non-Bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis

Pathology of the Heart II · SDL + ELS

5.1 Organisms & their sources

OrganismNormal Flora OfTypical SourceVirulence
Streptococcus viridansOral cavityDental procedures, poor dental hygiene, damaged/abnormal valvesLower
Staphylococcus aureusSkinIV drug use, prosthetic valve implantation (immediate or delayed)Higher
Staphylococcus epidermidisSkinProsthetic valve implantation (immediate)Lower
EnterococcusGI tractGI procedures/infectionsVariable
Two key sources to remember IV drug use and prosthetic valve implantation account for the large majority of infective endocarditis (IE) cases across organisms.

5.2 How vegetations form & what they cause

Endocardial injury triggers a healing response of platelets and fibrin. Circulating bacteria adhere to this site and proliferate, building up into friable vegetations. Ongoing tissue damage from the bacteria (and the immune response to them) further grows the vegetation. Consequences: valve destruction (affecting sufficiency) and embolization to distal sites (septic emboli, stroke).

5.3 Duke Criteria

CategoryExamples
Pathologic criteriaMicroorganisms found within a vegetation; embolus from a vegetation; explanted prosthetic valve/device showing infection
Major clinical criteriaPositive blood culture; imaging showing a valvular mass/abscess; new valvular regurgitation; direct visualization at surgery
Minor clinical criteriaPredisposing lesion/prosthetic valve/IV drug use; fever; vascular phenomena (emboli, infarcts, aneurysm, hemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots); microbiologic evidence not meeting major criteria

Diagnosis requires 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria — multiple manifestations are required because any single finding (e.g., a positive blood culture) could reflect infection elsewhere in the body; combining criteria increases diagnostic specificity.

5.4 Infective endocarditis vs. non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)

FeatureInfective EndocarditisNBTE
OrganismsPresentSterile — none present
SizeLarge, bulkySmall
TextureFriableBland
Tissue damage/inflammationExtensiveMinimal to none
AssociationBacteremia (IVDU, dental/GI procedures, prosthetic valves)Malignancy, hypercoagulable states
Practice Questions — Section 5

1. A 44-year-old IV drug user presents with fever and a new holosystolic murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Echocardiogram shows a large, friable vegetation on the tricuspid valve. Which set of Duke criteria is most directly satisfied by the blood culture and echocardiographic findings?

Explanation: A positive blood culture and imaging evidence of a veginal mass are each major Duke criteria; together they satisfy the "2 major criteria" pathway to diagnosis without needing any minor criteria.

2. A patient with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma is found incidentally to have small, sterile, non-destructive vegetations along the mitral valve line of closure with no organisms on culture. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation: Small, bland, sterile vegetations without tissue destruction in the setting of an underlying malignancy (a hypercoagulable state) is the classic presentation of NBTE, in contrast to the large, friable, organism-laden vegetations of infective endocarditis.

3. A patient develops infective endocarditis three months after a mechanical aortic valve replacement. Which organism is most classically associated with this delayed post-prosthetic timeframe?

Explanation: S. aureus is associated with prosthetic valve infection occurring at essentially any point after implantation (immediate or long-term), whereas S. epidermidis is classically tied to the immediate perioperative period specifically.

6. Cardiac Tumors

Pathology of the Heart II · SDL

6.1 Myxoma vs. rhabdomyoma

FeatureMyxomaRhabdomyoma
PopulationAdultsChildren
OriginMesenchymal cellsCardiac muscle cells
FrequencyMost common primary cardiac tumor in adultsAssociated with tuberous sclerosis
LocationLeft atrium (typically)Myocardium
Classic effect“Ball-valve” obstruction → episodic syncopeVariable, may cause outflow obstruction

6.2 Rhabdomyoma & tuberous sclerosis

Rhabdomyoma is associated with mutations in TSC1/TSC2, which normally regulate mTOR (a growth/proliferation-promoting protein). A loss-of-function mutation removes this brake on mTOR signaling, producing uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation.

6.3 Which cancers metastasize to the heart, and why

Cardiac metastases arise more readily from leukemia and lung cancer than from liver cancer:

  • Leukemia is a blood-borne cancer — as blood circulates through the heart, malignant cells readily seed cardiac tissue by simple proximity.
  • Lung cancer is anatomically adjacent to the heart, allowing direct invasion, lymphatic spread, and hematogenous spread into cardiac tissue.
  • Liver cancer is more distant, so metastatic cells are more likely to seed other organs before reaching the heart.
Liver → heart, indirectly Even though hepatic metastasis to the heart is uncommon, liver tumors can still produce cardiac lesions indirectly: metastatic liver lesions can secrete excess serotonin, which stimulates fibrous plaque formation on the heart — carcinoid heart disease.
Practice Questions — Section 6

1. A 58-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of syncope that resolve with positional changes. Echocardiogram reveals a pedunculated, gelatinous mass in the left atrium prolapsing through the mitral valve. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation: Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, classically arising in the LA and producing a "ball-valve" obstruction of the mitral orifice with positional syncope, as described here.

2. A 2-year-old with hypopigmented skin macules and infantile spasms is found to have a cardiac mass on echocardiogram obtained after a seizure workup. Which gene pathway is most likely disrupted?

Explanation: This vignette describes tuberous sclerosis (hypopigmented macules, seizures) with an associated cardiac rhabdomyoma. TSC1/TSC2 normally inhibit mTOR; loss-of-function mutations remove this brake, driving uncontrolled proliferation.

3. A patient with carcinoid syndrome from a liver-metastatic neuroendocrine tumor develops right-sided valvular fibrous plaques. What substance secreted by the metastatic tumor is responsible?

Explanation: Hepatic carcinoid metastases secrete excess serotonin, which stimulates fibrous plaque deposition on cardiac valves (classically right-sided, since the liver drains via the systemic/hepatic vein before the lung can metabolize the serotonin) — carcinoid heart disease.

7. Cardiomyopathy

Pathology of the Heart III · SDL + ELS

7.1 Structure = function: why some cardiomyopathies impair systole and others diastole

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) impairs systolic function: as the heart dilates, contractility falls and the heart can't pump effectively. Hypertrophic (HCM) and restrictive (RCM) cardiomyopathy both stiffen the heart from increased fibrosis/hypertrophy, impairing diastolic filling instead.

FeatureDilated CMHypertrophic CMRestrictive CM
Primary defectSystolic dysfunctionDiastolic dysfunction ± outflow obstructionDiastolic dysfunction (stiff walls)
Chamber sizeDilatedThick walls, small/normal cavityNormal size, thick/stiff walls
LVEF (approx.)~20% (reduced)~65% (preserved/hyperdynamic)~40% (mildly reduced)
Classic genetic driverTitin mutationβ-myosin heavy chain mutationTransthyretin mutation (amyloid)
Microscopic clueAttenuated, degenerating myocytes; interstitial fibrosisMyofiber disarray, hypertrophied myocytesAmyloid deposits (Congo red+) or other infiltrate

7.2 Asymmetric septal hypertrophy & sudden cardiac death

Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is disproportionate thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the rest of the LV wall — the hallmark of HCM. During exertion, this can obstruct the LV outflow tract, impair diastolic filling, reduce systemic oxygenation, and provoke myocardial ischemia and ventricular arrhythmias — all of which can culminate in sudden cardiac death, classically in young, otherwise healthy athletes.

Case — collegiate athlete, sudden collapse A 19-year-old collegiate basketball player collapses suddenly during a game and cannot be resuscitated. He had no known medical history but had experienced several episodes of exertional lightheadedness over the past year. Autopsy reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Post-mortem genetic testing reveals a mutation in the gene for β-myosin heavy chain.

Reasoning: β-myosin heavy chain is a core component of the cardiac sarcomere. A mutation impairs normal sarcomere contractility, and the heart compensates by hypertrophying to maintain cardiac output — producing the asymmetric septal hypertrophy of HCM. During exertion, this hypertrophied septum obstructs LV outflow, precipitating the arrhythmia responsible for sudden cardiac death.

7.3 Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy

CauseMechanism
Coxsackie B infectionViral myocarditis → myocyte damage & inflammation → fibrosis → DCM
AlcoholDirect myocardial toxicity + thiamine deficiency impairing cardiac metabolism → progressive myocyte injury
Daunorubicin / DoxorubicinAnthracyclines generate reactive oxygen species → DNA/mitochondrial damage → myocyte dysfunction, death, fibrosis
PregnancyMultifactorial: genetic predisposition, hypertension, hormonal changes, immune dysregulation, oxidative stress
Extreme psychological distressTakotsubo (“broken heart”) cardiomyopathy: catecholamine surge → myocyte toxicity & systolic dysfunction, can progress to DCM
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy A surge of catecholamines (classically after acute emotional or physical stress) produces transient apical ballooning of the LV with systolic dysfunction, mimicking an MI but with unremarkable coronary angiography. Named for its resemblance to a Japanese octopus trap (tako-tsubo).

7.4 Restrictive cardiomyopathy: mechanisms of stiffening

CauseMechanism
AmyloidosisExtracellular amyloid deposits stiffen the myocardium, impairing diastolic filling
SarcoidosisGranulomatous inflammation & subsequent fibrosis stiffen the heart
Endomyocardial fibrosisFibrosis of the endocardium from nutritional deficiency or parasitic infection
Thoracic radiationRadiation-induced fibrosis and stiffening
HemochromatosisIron deposition within the myocardium
Practice Questions — Section 7

1. A 45-year-old woman with a 10-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with progressive dyspnea and an echocardiogram showing a markedly dilated LV with an ejection fraction of 22%. Which additional deficiency commonly compounds alcohol's direct myocardial toxicity in this setting?

Explanation: Chronic alcohol use commonly causes thiamine deficiency, which independently impairs cardiac metabolism and compounds the direct myocardial toxicity of alcohol and its metabolites, together producing alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy.

2. A 68-year-old woman develops sudden chest pain and dyspnea shortly after receiving news of her husband's death. ECG shows nonspecific ST changes, troponin is mildly elevated, and coronary angiography is unremarkable. Echocardiogram shows apical ballooning of the LV. What is the underlying mechanism?

Explanation: This is Takotsubo ("broken heart") cardiomyopathy, triggered by an acute catecholamine surge (often after severe emotional stress) that is directly toxic to myocytes, producing transient apical ballooning and systolic dysfunction despite normal coronary arteries.

3. A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic kidney disease and a monoclonal gammopathy develops progressive dyspnea. Echocardiogram shows a non-dilated heart with thickened walls, biatrial enlargement, and preserved ejection fraction. A biopsy is stained with Congo red. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation: Biatrial enlargement with a non-dilated, thick-walled, stiff ventricle and preserved EF, in a patient at risk for amyloid deposition (monoclonal gammopathy), with Congo red staining performed, points to restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis.

8. Myocarditis

Pathology of the Heart III · SDL + ELS

8.1 Infectious causes

Common infectious causes of myocarditis include Coxsackie B, influenza, HIV, Lyme disease, rubella, SARS-CoV-2, Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), and trichinosis, among others.

8.2 Microscopic patterns point to different causes

Not every case of myocarditis is infectious, and the microscopic infiltrate itself can point you toward a mechanism:

PatternMicroscopic ClueAssociated Cause
Parasitic myocarditisIntracellular organism visible within myocytes (e.g., trypanosome pseudocysts)Chagas disease
Lymphocytic myocarditisLymphocyte/mononuclear infiltrate, minimal eosinophils or giant cellsViral infection or general tissue injury (most common pattern overall)
Hypersensitivity myocarditisAbundant eosinophils (hot pink, granular cytoplasm) infiltrating the myocardiumDrug hypersensitivity reaction
Giant cell myocarditisMultinucleated giant cells (fused macrophages), granuloma-likeIdiopathic/autoimmune; aggressive, often rapidly progressive

8.3 Acute myocarditis → chronic disease

As myocarditis-associated inflammation heals, it produces cell death and fibrosis of the myocardium and surrounding tissue. This fibrosis and the resulting impaired contractile function can progress to cardiomyopathy (typically dilated), heart failure, arrhythmia, or eventually sudden cardiac death.

Practice Questions — Section 8

1. A patient recently returned from rural South America presents with dilated cardiomyopathy. Endomyocardial biopsy shows an intracellular organism within a myocyte. What is the most likely causative organism?

Explanation: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is endemic to rural Latin America and can cause chronic myocarditis with intracellular trypanosome pseudocysts visible on biopsy, progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy.

2. A patient started on a new antibiotic one week ago develops fever, rash, and new heart failure symptoms. Myocardial biopsy shows a dense inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation: An eosinophil-rich infiltrate temporally linked to a new medication is characteristic of hypersensitivity myocarditis, a drug reaction rather than a direct infection.

3. A previously healthy 30-year-old man develops rapidly progressive heart failure and ventricular arrhythmias. Biopsy shows extensive myocardial inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and no identifiable organism. Which myocarditis pattern does this represent?

Explanation: Multinucleated giant cells on biopsy without an identifiable infectious organism, in the setting of rapidly progressive heart failure/arrhythmia, is classic for giant cell myocarditis — typically idiopathic/autoimmune and more aggressive than the lymphocytic pattern.

9. Congestive Heart Failure

Pathology of the Heart IV · SDL + ELS

9.1 Compensatory mechanisms — and how each becomes maladaptive

MechanismCompensationHow It Becomes Maladaptive
Frank-Starling mechanismThe heart dilates in response to ↑ filling volumes, initially increasing contractilityChronic volume-overload overwhelms this mechanism → progressive myocardial contractile dysfunction
Neurohumoral activationSignaling systems (RAAS, sympathetic) regulate CV function acutely in response to stressChronic activation stimulates remodeling → impaired diastolic and/or systolic function → heart failure
Myocardial (hypertrophic) remodelingThe heart hypertrophies to increase cardiac outputHypertrophy raises O₂ demand beyond what the (unchanged) vascular supply can meet → ↓ compliance and fibrosis → heart failure

9.2 Cellular hypertrophy, step by step

Pressure-overload stress triggers myocytes to re-express immediate-early genes (stimulating growth and contractile protein expression) and sometimes fetal genes. As cardiomyocytes enlarge, so does the myocardium as a whole. This increases myocyte oxygen demand without a matched increase in vascularization → ischemia, fibrosis, and eventual heart failure. In parallel, myocardial fibroblasts increase extracellular matrix deposition, further contributing to size increase and fibrosis.

9.3 Forward vs. backward failure

TypeMechanismConsequence
Forward failureDiminished ability of the heart to pump blood↓ Cardiac output and tissue perfusion
Backward failurePooling of blood into the venous system upstream of the failing chamberPulmonary or systemic edema

9.4 LVEF: why it tracks systolic, not diastolic, dysfunction

LVEF describes how much blood leaves the heart with each contraction. Because systole is the contraction phase, LVEF is far more sensitive to changes in systolic function (HFrEF — Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction) than to diastolic function. Diastolic dysfunction reflects impaired ventricular filling, which does not by itself alter contractility — this is HFpEF (Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction).

9.5 Right-sided heart failure: systemic congestion

Organ SystemManifestation
LiverCongestive hepatomegaly (“nutmeg liver”), cardiac cirrhosis
ExtremitiesPeripheral edema
Peritoneal cavityAscites
SpleenSplenomegaly

9.6 BNP: the reconciliation question

Case — chronic systolic heart failure A 70-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure presents with worsening dyspnea and lower-extremity edema. BNP is markedly elevated. Elevated BNP is associated with a poor prognosis in this patient — how do you reconcile this with BNP's normal physiologic role in maintaining cardiovascular homeostasis?

Reasoning: Systolic heart failure → LV dysfunction/HFrEF → the heart attempts to adapt through increased pressure or volume → LV wall stress → BNP release, which physiologically counters RAAS (promoting vasodilation and natriuresis) to reduce blood pressure and cardiac workload. In advanced heart failure, however, these compensatory efforts are insufficient to resolve the underlying stress, so BNP continues to be released in a futile effort to overcome it — making a persistently high BNP a marker of just how much stress the ventricle is under, and therefore a marker of poor prognosis, even though the hormone itself is doing exactly what it is supposed to do.
Practice Questions — Section 9

1. A patient with long-standing aortic stenosis develops progressive dyspnea. Echocardiogram shows preserved LVEF but impaired ventricular relaxation and filling. Which term best classifies this heart failure?

Explanation: Preserved LVEF with impaired diastolic filling is HFpEF (Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction) — the ejection fraction, a systolic measurement, remains normal because the defect is in relaxation/filling, not contraction.

2. A patient with chronic right heart failure develops tender hepatomegaly with a mottled, "nutmeg" appearance on imaging, along with lower extremity edema and ascites. Which mechanism best explains the hepatic finding?

Explanation: Right heart failure causes systemic venous congestion; elevated pressure transmitted back through the IVC/hepatic veins produces centrilobular congestion, giving the classic mottled "nutmeg liver" appearance (and, if chronic, cardiac cirrhosis).

3. In a patient with pressure-overload hypertrophy, why does the hypertrophied myocardium become progressively more ischemic over time even without epicardial coronary artery disease?

Explanation: As myocytes hypertrophy in response to pressure-overload, the myocardial mass and its oxygen demand increase, but the coronary microvasculature does not expand proportionately — producing a relative (demand-supply mismatch) ischemia that drives fibrosis even without epicardial disease.

10. Ischemic Heart Disease

Pathology of the Heart IV · SDL + ELS

10.1 IHD vs. CHF

Ischemic heart disease (IHD) occurs when the heart's own oxygen demand outstrips its supply. Congestive heart failure occurs when the heart cannot meet the oxygen (perfusion) demands of the rest of the body. Both are oxygen-deficit states, but IHD describes the effect on the heart itself, while CHF describes the downstream systemic effect — and IHD frequently progresses to CHF.

10.2 Occlusion site & extent determine the infarct pattern

The site of occlusion determines the location/pattern of ischemia; the extent of occlusion determines the size and depth of the resulting infarct. Each coronary artery supplies a defined perfusion territory, and the most distal portion of that territory (furthest from the arterial supply) infarcts earliest.

10.3 STEMI vs. NSTEMI

TermECG PatternUnderlying Infarct
STEMIST-segment elevationTransmural infarct from complete coronary occlusion
NSTEMINo ST elevationSubendocardial infarct from incomplete/transient occlusion

10.4 Stable vs. unstable angina

FeatureStable AnginaUnstable Angina
CauseChronic fixed stenosis (atherosclerosis)Acute plaque disruption, thrombosis, embolism, or vasospasm
TriggerExertion; relieved by rest or nitroglycerinIncreasingly frequent, prolonged, or severe; occurs at low exertion or rest
Risk of imminent MILow (though severe/chronic cases raise risk of heart failure, arrhythmia, sudden death)High

10.5 Cardiac biomarkers: troponin vs. CK-MB

Troponin regulates calcium-mediated actin-myosin contraction; as ischemic myocytes undergo necrosis, troponin is released into circulation. It is the most sensitive and specific biomarker for myocardial injury. CK-MB is a myocardial enzyme involved in ATP regeneration during contraction, also released with cell death, but it is less specific (can also rise with skeletal muscle injury) and resolves much faster.

BiomarkerRisesPeaksReturns to Baseline
Troponin2–4 hr24–48 hr~7–10 days
CK-MB6–12 hr~24 hr~48 hr
Why CK-MB is still useful despite being less sensitive Because CK-MB resolves so much faster than troponin, a re-elevated CK-MB in a patient with a recent prior MI (whose troponin is already elevated and slow to clear) is a useful clue for reinfarction — troponin alone can't distinguish a new event from the tail of the first one.

10.6 Reperfusion injury

Reperfusion injury describes complications of therapeutic reperfusion (thrombolysis, angioplasty, CABG) of previously ischemic myocardium:

MechanismDetail
Mitochondrial dysfunction↑ mitochondrial membrane permeability from prior damage → mitochondrial rupture on reperfusion → released contents trigger apoptosis
Myocyte hypercontractureCalcium accumulated in damaged myocytes causes uncontrolled, excessive contraction on reperfusion → cytoskeletal damage & cell death
Free radicalsReperfusion/reoxygenation rapidly generates free radicals that damage membrane proteins/phospholipids
Inflammation (“no reflow”)Immune cell/platelet aggregation at the injury site can itself block adequate reperfusion of the area

10.7 Complications of myocardial infarction

ComplicationDetail
Contractile dysfunction↓ pump function proportional to infarct size
Right ventricular infarctionEspecially with RCA occlusion
Myocardial ruptureSeptal, papillary muscle, or ventricular free wall (see 10.8)
ArrhythmiaTachycardia, bradycardia, VFib, AFib, asystole, heart block
PericarditisFibrinous, post-infarction
Mural thrombosisRisk of systemic embolization
Ventricular aneurysmThinned, scarred wall balloons outward
Progressive heart failureFrom cumulative loss of contractile mass

10.8 Myocardial rupture — the highest-risk window & three types

Risk of rupture is highest around 3–7 days post-infarct, when the infarcted tissue has undergone extensive coagulative necrosis and neutrophilic digestion but has not yet been reinforced by mature granulation tissue/collagen — the myocardium is at its structurally weakest.

TypeConsequence
Septal ruptureVentricular septal defect with L→R shunting
Papillary muscle ruptureAcute mitral regurgitation/insufficiency
Ventricular free wall ruptureHemopericardium → cardiac tamponade → sudden death

10.9 Arrhythmias

ArrhythmiaDescription
TachycardiaFast heart rate
BradycardiaSlow heart rate (sick sinus syndrome)
Ventricular fibrillationChaotic depolarization; irregular, nonfunctional ventricular contraction
Atrial fibrillationIndependent, sporadic atrial depolarization; “irregularly irregular” rhythm
AsystoleNo electrical activity
Heart blockIndependent contraction of atria and ventricles

10.10 The MI timeline: biochemical, microscopic, and gross evolution

This is the single highest-yield timeline in cardiac pathology — know the order cold.

TimeBiochemicalMicroscopicGross
0–0.5 hrATP depletion, shift to anaerobic metabolism, ↓ myocyte contractility——
0.5–4 hrTroponin begins to rise (~2–4 hr)(E) Wavy myofibers—
4–12 hrCK-MB begins to rise (~6–12 hr)(H) Interstitial edema; (C) hemorrhage; coagulative necrosis begins—
12–24 hr—(B) Coagulative necrosis progressing; neutrophil infiltration begins—
1–3 daysTroponin & CK-MB peak (~24 hr); CK-MB returns to baseline (~48 hr)(D) Loss of cross-striation; (A) neutrophil infiltration (density increases through day 2–3)(2) Dark mottling with central yellow-tan infarct
3–7 days—(G) Neutrophil karyorrhexis(1) Hyperemic border with central yellow-tan softening — highest rupture risk
7–14 daysTroponin returns to baseline(I) Extensive granulation tissue (~7 days)(4) Maximally yellow-tan and soft, depressed red-tan margins
2–8 weeks—(J) Collagen deposition, decreasing cellularity—
>2 months—(F) Dense collagen(3) Dense white scar
Case — dating an infarct grossly A 67-year-old man dies shortly after arriving in the ED with a suspected MI (elevated troponin and CK-MB). Autopsy reveals an infarct with a hyperemic border and central yellow-tan softening.

Based on gross appearance alone, this infarct is approximately 3–7 days old — the hyperemic border with central yellow-tan softening is the classic gross description for this window.

Follow-up reasoning: Troponin stays elevated for days after infarction, but CK-MB normally resolves by ~48 hours. If CK-MB is still elevated shortly before death in a patient with a first infarct old enough to be in the 3–7 day window, the most likely explanation is a second (more recent) infarction — not shown on this particular gross section — since CK-MB can also rise from other causes like skeletal muscle injury, but in this clinical context (recent prior MI, high troponin, no other trauma) reinfarction is the more likely explanation.
Practice Questions — Section 10

1. An autopsy on a patient who died 5 days after an acute MI shows a soft, friable, yellow-tan infarct with a hyperemic border. Which complication is this patient at the highest risk for during this window?

Explanation: Days 3–7 post-MI is when the infarcted myocardium is maximally soft and friable (extensive coagulative necrosis and neutrophilic digestion without yet having mature granulation tissue for structural support) — the peak window for myocardial (especially free wall) rupture.

2. A 60-year-old man's ECG shows ST-segment elevations, and coronary angiography reveals complete occlusion of the LAD. Which infarct pattern is expected?

Explanation: Complete occlusion of a major coronary artery (here, the LAD) produces a transmural (full-thickness) infarct in that vessel's perfusion territory, which manifests as ST-elevation (STEMI) on ECG.

3. Histology of an infarct shows myofibers with preserved cell outlines, loss of nuclei, and hypereosinophilic cytoplasm, with a dense band of neutrophils undergoing karyorrhexis at the infarct border. What is the most likely time since infarction?

Explanation: Coagulative necrosis with neutrophil karyorrhexis (fragmenting neutrophil nuclei) is characteristic of the 3–7 day window, when the acute neutrophilic response is winding down but granulation tissue has not yet replaced the necrotic zone.

4. A patient develops a new holosystolic murmur and acute pulmonary edema four days after an inferoposterior STEMI. Which complication best explains this presentation?

Explanation: A new holosystolic murmur with acute pulmonary edema in the days following an MI (especially inferoposterior, which supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle) suggests papillary muscle rupture causing acute, severe mitral regurgitation. Septal rupture would suggest a VSD (harsh murmur with left-to-right shunt); free wall rupture presents with tamponade and sudden death, not a murmur.

5. Two days after an MI, a patient's CK-MB has already returned toward baseline while troponin remains markedly elevated. Which property of troponin best explains this difference?

Explanation: Troponin and CK-MB are both released with myocyte necrosis, but troponin remains detectably elevated for roughly 7–10 days, while CK-MB clears by about 48 hours — making troponin more useful for confirming a recent MI, and CK-MB more useful for detecting reinfarction within days of the first event.
